\label{sec:results}

\begin{guide}
Write each subsection in the same three steps: (1) one sentence saying what the table

\todo{Opening paragraph: what is compared, over how many datasets, over how many
seeds, and which numbers are mine versus published.}

{This section compares 66 model variants (\seanet{} encoders paired with \seanet{}
and \millet{} pooling heads, plus the FCN, ResNet and InceptionTime baselines) over up
to 129 datasets: \webtraffic{} and the 128-dataset \ucr{} archive
(\Cref{sec:setup:data}). Two seed regimes are used, and I say this once here rather
than repeating it in every caption. The 66-model \ucr{} sweep is single-seed
(seed~$=0$) throughout, for the reasons given in \Cref{sec:setup:protocol}. On
\webtraffic{}, three models were re-run for two extra seeds after the main sweep --
my two headline variants and the re-trained \millet{} baseline -- so those three rows
report a real mean $\pm$ std over 3 seeds; the ResNet and FCN baselines only have the
one \webtraffic{} seed. Every number I present as ``mine'' or ``re-trained'' comes
from my own training runs with my own recipe (\Cref{sec:setup:protocol}); every number
marked ``published'' is copied from \citet{early2024millet} and is never averaged or
combined with a number I produced myself (\Cref{sec:setup:baselines}).}

\todo{Two or three sentences reading \Cref{tab:web_main}: which model wins on
accuracy, which on explanation quality, and what it costs in parameters. If the two

{Both proposed heads beat every re-trained baseline on all three metrics at once,
while using between 7$\times$ and 10$\times$ fewer parameters than the re-trained
\millet{} baseline. \texttt{seanet\_bottleneck\_topk} is the more convincing of the
two: it has the highest accuracy (0.947) \emph{and} the highest NDCG@$n$ (0.773), it
is the smaller of my two models (41{,}324 params), and its seed-to-seed std is the
tightest in the table. \texttt{seanet\_inputgate\_adaptive} edges it on mean AOPCR
(2.651 vs.\ 2.621), but that gap is well inside one standard deviation of either
model, so I do not read it as a real win -- and its own numbers are far noisier
across seeds (accuracy ranges from 0.88 to 0.938 across the three seeds, against
\texttt{seanet\_bottleneck\_topk}'s narrow 0.938--0.966). So accuracy and explanation
quality are \emph{not} split across two different models here: one head
(\texttt{seanet\_bottleneck\_topk}) wins on both, and is also the cheaper and more
stable of the two -- a cleaner headline result than I expected going in.}

\todo{Two or three sentences reading \Cref{tab:ucr_accuracy}.}

{This table tells a different story than \Cref{tab:web_main}: on the 85-dataset
archive, my re-trained \millet{} baseline has both the best mean accuracy (0.8274)
and the best average rank (12.50) of the five models here, and every alternative --
both of my proposed heads and the ResNet/FCN baselines -- loses more datasets than it
wins against it. I do not think this contradicts the \webtraffic{} result; I think it
shows the limit of screening on one dataset (\Cref{sec:setup:data}): both proposed
heads were selected because they did well on \webtraffic{}, which does not guarantee
they generalise best across 85 very different \ucr{} datasets. \seanet{} is still
competitive here (within 1--2 accuracy points of the baseline, at a fraction of the
parameters) and clearly beats the plain ResNet/FCN backbones on rank, but ``clearly
ahead everywhere'' is a claim \Cref{tab:web_main} alone cannot support, and this table
is the honest correction to it. Against the published number (0.8445), my re-trained
\millet{} baseline lands close but slightly below it (0.8274), within the kind of gap
a different recipe and a single seed can easily produce (\Cref{sec:disc:reading}); my
own two heads sit a little further back again. None of these differences are large
enough, on a single seed, for me to call them a real ranking between ``my re-trained
baseline'' and ``the paper'' -- only that both are in the same ballpark, which is the
sanity check \Cref{sec:setup:baselines} was for.}

\todo{Two or three sentences: does a better explanation cost accuracy here? Which
pooling head concentrates the evidence best, and does that match the intention behind
its design (\Cref{sec:pool:topk}, \Cref{sec:pool:dsmil})?}

{Not for \texttt{seanet\_bottleneck\_topk}: it has the best NDCG@$n$ of the three
\emph{and} the best accuracy, so nothing was traded away to get a sharper
explanation -- exactly what Top-$k$ pooling (\Cref{sec:pool:topk}) was designed to do,
since averaging only the $k$ most decisive time steps both concentrates the evidence
and removes noise the classifier would otherwise have to average over.
\texttt{seanet\_inputgate\_adaptive} does show a real cost: it has the best mean AOPCR
of the three (by a small, not clearly significant margin over
\texttt{seanet\_bottleneck\_topk} -- \Cref{tab:web_main}), but it pays for that with
both lower accuracy and by far the largest std of the three, on every metric. My
reading is that Adaptive class-wise pooling (\Cref{sec:pool:adaptive}) is a smoother,
learned mean--max blend that can end up isolating evidence about as sharply as Top-$k$
does on a good seed, but -- unlike Top-$k$'s fixed, hard selection -- how far it leans
towards ``max'' is itself something the optimiser has to learn, which is one more
thing that can land differently between seeds.}

% slightly from its trained params (423,707): the pooling head's parameter count scales with
% n_classes, and the profiling proxy uses 5 classes instead of WebTraffic's 10).
% Train time is wall-clock to convergence (includes early stopping), NOT a per-step cost measure --

\todo{Two sentences: the parameter reduction as a percentage, and whether it also
translates into faster inference (it does not always -- say so if it does not).}

{\texttt{seanet\_bottleneck\_topk} cuts parameters by 90\% relative to the re-trained
\millet{} baseline (41{,}324 vs.\ 423{,}707, a 10.3$\times$ reduction) and that
translates cleanly into inference speed too: 0.631\,ms vs.\ 1.031\,ms, about
1.6$\times$ faster. \texttt{seanet\_inputgate\_adaptive} is the counter-example the
guide above asks for: it is also 86\% smaller than \millet{} (58{,}102 params,
7.3$\times$ fewer) but is \emph{2.5$\times$ slower} at inference (2.594\,ms vs.\
1.031\,ms) despite having a fifth of the parameters and a fraction of the FLOPs --
smaller is clearly not always faster. I have not confirmed the exact cause, but the
input gate this encoder adds (\texttt{seanet/features.py}, \texttt{InputGate}) applies
an extra per-time-step sigmoid gate before every block, which is cheap in FLOPs but
adds a sequential op the GPU may not parallelise as well as the plain convolutions the
other encoders use; I flag this as a real cost of that design rather than a
measurement artefact, since the FLOPs and param counts both say it should be cheap.}

{The model in the good corner (high accuracy, low parameter count) is

in the entire 66-model sweep -- with only 61{,}740 parameters, 4.4$\times$ fewer than
the re-trained \millet{} baseline (\Cref{tab:web_main}) at equal accuracy. A model is
Pareto-optimal on this plot if no other model is both smaller \emph{and} at least as
accurate; the dashed front joins those models, and every point off the front is
strictly dominated by one still on it.}

(105.97\,s, 112.98\,s, 132.95\,s) and for the re-trained \millet{} baseline (41.57\,s,
49.12\,s, 60.40\,s).}

  \figph[0.8]{\textbf{Figure X -- Training curves.} Training and validation loss
  against epoch for my best model and for the \millet{} baseline, on \webtraffic{},
  with the early-stopping epoch marked.}
  \caption{\todo{Caption: one sentence on what the curves show.}}
  \label{fig:curves}
\end{figure}
\note{This figure needs the same per-epoch history as the loss columns above
(\texttt{model.history} in MLflow), which I do not have access to in this session --
I have not drawn it and have not guessed at what it would show. To produce it: open
the real MLflow store the Grid'5000 runs were logged to, pull the per-epoch monitored
loss for one \webtraffic{} run of each model (the metric \texttt{val\_acc}/the
history list logged by \texttt{seanet/train.py}'s \texttt{fit()}), and plot both
curves with the epoch where \texttt{epochs\_no\_improve} hit \texttt{patience}
(=60) marked.}

\todo{Two sentences reading \Cref{tab:losses} and \Cref{fig:curves}.}

{The one thing I can say from Training time alone: \texttt{seanet\_bottleneck\_topk}
consistently takes longer to converge than the re-trained \millet{} baseline (roughly
2--3$\times$, across all 3 seeds), even though it is over 10$\times$ smaller and
$11\times$ cheaper per step in FLOPs (\Cref{tab:cost}) -- consistent with the
per-step-vs-wall-clock distinction already noted in \Cref{sec:res:cost}, and a
reminder that a smaller model is not automatically a faster one to \emph{train}, only
cheaper to \emph{run}. Whether this is because it needs more epochs to reach the same
loss, or because early stopping simply behaves differently for the two loss
landscapes, is exactly the question \Cref{fig:curves} would answer, and I do not have
the data to answer it honestly here.}

\subsection{Ablations}
\label{sec:res:ablation}

\begin{guide}
Keep only the ablation that answers the main question: does the gain come from the
encoder, from the pooling head, or from their combination? The rest of the ablations
go to \Cref{app:ablations}.
\end{guide}

\begin{figure}[h]
  \centering
  \figph[0.8]{\textbf{Figure X -- Encoder $\times$ pooling head grid.} Heat map of
  \webtraffic{} accuracy for every encoder (rows) and every pooling head (columns), so
  the two effects can be separated.}
  \caption{\todo{Caption: how to read the grid, and which row/column stands out.}}
  \label{fig:ablation_grid}
\end{figure}

{Read each cell as the \webtraffic{} accuracy of that (encoder, pooling head) pair;
darker is better. No single row or column is uniformly dark -- the best cell in the
grid (\texttt{sea\_mstcn\_sep\_gated} $\times$ \texttt{sea\_topk\_conjunctive}, 0.954)
is not in the row or column with the best \emph{average}, which is exactly the
interaction effect described below.}
% Diagram brief / data note for fig:ablation_grid: the pdf already exists
% (results/paper_figures/02_ablation/ablation_encoder_pooling_grid.pdf) -- this is describing what
% is already drawn, not proposing a new figure. Marginal means below computed directly from
% results/SEA_NET/leaderboard.csv (grouping the 66 rows by encoder and by pooling, mean web_acc).

\todo{Three sentences: the effect of the encoder alone, the effect of the head alone,
and whether the best pair is the pair of the two individual bests (often it is not).}

{On their own, the pooling head matters about as much as the encoder does: grouped by
head, mean \webtraffic{} accuracy (excluding the single-sample \millet{} pooling
heads, not a fair comparison at $n=1$) spans from 0.744 (Dual-stream, $n=4$) to 0.921
(Class-wise conjunctive, $n=10$); grouped by encoder (same exclusion for the
single-sample baseline backbones), it spans from 0.858 (Spike/trend, $n=7$) to 0.937
(\texttt{sea\_multiscale\_channels}, $n=4$) -- a similar-sized range. Neither the best
encoder by this marginal average (\texttt{sea\_multiscale\_channels}, 0.937) nor the
best head (Class-wise conjunctive, 0.921) is the one that actually appears in the best
row: the true best model
(\texttt{seanet\_gated\_mean\_topk}, 0.954, \Cref{fig:pareto}) pairs the Gated encoder
(mean 0.902, mid-table on its own) with Top-$k$ pooling (mean 0.904, also mid-table on
its own). Neither component looks exceptional in isolation; the pair is the best
result in the whole sweep. That is the main lesson of this grid: the gain is not
simply additive, and picking the best row of the grid required trying the
combination, not just the two best marginals.}
